passage.title: The Many Editions of a Single Song
paragraphs: A folk song recorded in two neighboring villages may share a melody while telling noticeably different stories. One singer supplies a village name where another mentions a river; one ends with a reunion where another describes a departure. For an editor preparing a collection, these differences pose a practical problem. A reader expects to see a song printed in one place and may assume that whatever appears beneath the title is the song itself. Yet selecting a single rendition as authoritative gives unusual power to a decision that may have depended on access, timing or the recording equipment an editor happened to bring.

Older collections sometimes resolved this difficulty by combining verses from several performances. The resulting song could seem exceptionally coherent because repeated lines were removed and gaps filled with material from a different singer. Later readers, unaware of those interventions, might confidently use the printed version as evidence of how the song was performed. The edition's fluency thus helped disguise the sequence of editorial choices that produced it. This does not mean the resulting text was useless. It may have been ideal for stage performance or for teaching a tune to children. Its suitability simply depended on a purpose that needed to be stated.

A small archive has experimented with a format that retains several performances under the same title. Instead of putting variations in a separate appendix, the archive places short recordings and their transcriptions next to one another. A brief note explains which recordings were made for a visiting collector and which came from an occasion where the audience already knew the refrain. That distinction can help account for a difference in tempo or the length of a pause. It also underscores that even a recording preserves an event arranged under particular circumstances rather than a song removed from time.

This solution introduces another editorial difficulty. Presenting three accessible performances can suggest that those three exhaust the tradition, while dozens of undocumented occasions remain unavailable. An archive also needs a searchable title, even when singers use different names or none at all. The modern editor therefore still exercises discretion. What changes is the visibility of some decisions and the reader's opportunity to hear the material on which those decisions rest. In that respect the archive resembles an edition of a historical document: its task includes making the evidence easier to inspect without implying that the act of arranging it has left the evidence untouched.

questions.prompt: What principle regarding folk songs underlies the passage as a whole?
options: Folk songs can be archived accurately only without searchable titles.
An edition should make the relationship between its presentation and the performance evidence visible.
A single rendition should always displace variants when it is complete.
Printed collections should serve only as rehearsal materials.

explanation.correct: The problems with composite texts and the new archive both concern inspectable choices.

distractors.0: Searchable titles remain a necessity and illustrate unavoidable decisions.
distractors.2: The author shows how treating one rendition as definitive can give accidental factors undue influence.
distractors.3: Rehearsal is one legitimate use among others.

questions.prompt: Why could the combined versions in older collections mislead future scholars?
options: They transcribed recordings made by the audiences themselves.
They always identified one of the source villages incorrectly.

explanation.correct: The polished sequence could be mistaken for a documented performance.

distractors.0: Their misleading effect concerns composition of the printed text, independent of recording personnel.
distractors.1: Incorrect place identification is not alleged.
distractors.3: Some repetitions were removed; the passage does not make this sweeping claim.

questions.prompt: How does the author evaluate the archive’s side-by-side format?

explanation.correct: The format increases transparency but still requires selection and naming.

distractors.1: The possibility of undocumented events explicitly limits this claim.
distractors.2: The author says the format puts accessible performances within reach.
distractors.3: The choices concern archival representation, not regulation of performers.

passage.title: Dunes with a Pulse
paragraphs: People who visit a desert once may remember its dunes as permanent features, as much a part of the landscape as a ridge of rock. Surveyors who return repeatedly find something less stable. Sand advances up the shallow face of a dune as wind drives grains in short hops. At the crest, some of the grains fall down a steep sheltered slope. The dune can thus migrate without carrying the same grains along for its whole journey. In a moving dune, the shape persists through the circulation of material. From an unmoving viewpoint, by contrast, the dune seems to be a single object sliding across the ground.

This circulation does not proceed at a steady rate. A wind too gentle to lift resting grains may sustain movement after other grains are already hopping, because incoming grains knock additional ones loose. Gusts that cross the initial threshold matter disproportionately. Rain temporarily binds grains together, so even windy hours may yield little transport on a recently wetted surface. The annual average wind speed, when considered alone, conceals these interruptions and bursts. Two locations with similar annual averages may therefore have very different patterns of sand movement.

A further complication is that dunes affect the airflow that moves them. A growing ridge diverts the wind, and the distortion can influence the transport of sand on a neighbouring ridge. When researchers observe a row of regularly spaced dunes, they do not necessarily need to invoke evenly spaced obstacles beneath the sand. The spacing can emerge while wind and dune shapes adjust to each other. Looking for buried obstacles may still be useful at a particular site, but regularity alone provides little warrant for assuming they exist.

This is why cautious reconstruction of desert history draws on more than the surface outline. The angles of layers exposed in sand pits may reveal former slip faces, and layers of different grain sizes can record changes in transport. Even these clues have limits. A new shift in prevailing winds can erode part of the record before depositing another set of layers. The evidence is therefore selective. A striking dune is both a present structure assembled by the latest winds and an imperfect archive of earlier conditions. Its interpretation requires thinking about which episodes preserved evidence and which erased it, as well as about the conditions that produced the shape visible today.

questions.prompt: How does the discussion of migrating dunes connect their present appearance with their past?
options: Dune positions are principally determined by regularly spaced buried obstacles.
Dunes are maintained by moving grains, and both ongoing transport and partial preservation shape what their current forms reveal.
Changes in grain size reveal the exact speed of every wind that ever crossed the desert.
A dune retains the same grains throughout its migration, enabling a full reconstruction of its origin.

explanation.correct: The passage explains changing airflow and the selective record created by deposition and erosion.

distractors.0: The text offers self-organized spacing and cautions against inferring obstacles from regularity.
distractors.2: Selective preservation prevents a complete chronological record.
distractors.3: The opening denies continuous membership of the same grains and the end explains erasure.

questions.prompt: Why might a brief storm move more sand than many hours of moderately windy weather at the same dry site?
options: A gust can initiate hopping, after which collisions dislodge grains at speeds too low to start transport unaided.
A storm eliminates the dune’s slip face before any movement begins.
Dry storm winds bind grains together in the same way that rain does.
Moderate wind always drives grains straight downward into the ground.

explanation.correct: The passage describes separate thresholds for starting and sustaining grain movement.

distractors.1: Eliminating the slip face is unnecessary for grain transport.
distractors.2: Wetting binds grains and opposes transport.
distractors.3: The ability to move sand varies with threshold and surface conditions.

questions.prompt: What attitude does the author take toward deductions drawn from regularly spaced dunes?
options: Unequivocal, insisting that regular spacing proves uniform underlying obstacles.
Indifferent, suggesting that there is nothing to explain in the first place.
Cautious, proposing an alternative mechanism and allowing site-specific tests.
Dismissive, calling further field investigation inadmissible.

explanation.correct: Regular spacing could emerge from interacting dunes or have another cause at a given site.

distractors.0: Regularity alone is judged insufficient evidence.
distractors.1: The origin of regular spacing is treated as an explanatory problem.
distractors.3: The text explicitly allows that investigating buried obstacles can be useful.

questions.prompt: In the sentence on buried obstacles, “warrant” is closest in meaning to what?
options: A reasonable basis.
A cause of erosion.
A measure of distance.
A formal ban.

explanation.correct: The visual pattern alone gives too little grounds for that conclusion.

distractors.1: The word evaluates an assumption rather than explaining sand removal.
distractors.2: Spacing is the topic, but the word denotes grounds for belief.
distractors.3: The author permits investigation and is discussing justification.

questions.prompt: What can make sand layers an incomplete record of previous winds?
options: All sand layers cease to move after the first rainfall.
Each grain always falls into the same former slip face.
A new wind regime can remove old layers before adding new ones.
Wind cannot cause layers of different grain sizes to form.

explanation.correct: Later erosion can destroy earlier evidence prior to renewed deposition.

distractors.0: Wetting can temporarily inhibit motion without making dunes permanently stable.
distractors.1: The passage describes migration and erosion instead of fixed grain positions.
distractors.3: Such layers are explicitly identified as clues to transport changes.
